claims.text: There is a blog post titled 'SST Runs on the Pulumi Engine: What It Means to Build on Pulumi' at /blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/ that provides a closer look at the engine mechanics behind SST's migration to Pulumi.
AWS CDK was a starting point for SST (Serverless Stack) but had limitations.
CDK tied SST's infrastructure to AWS.
Debugging was frustrating for SST due to CloudFormation templates.
Multi-cloud deployment was nearly impossible for SST when built on AWS CDK.
Pulumi lets SST offer a faster, more flexible, and provider-agnostic infrastructure experience.
SST was originally built on top of AWS's Cloud Development Kit (CDK).
AWS CDK allowed developers to define their infrastructure using TypeScript or Python.
With AWS CDK and CloudFormation, the infrastructure code is a code generator that produces an intermediary format (such as YAML or JSON) that is then executed to deploy resources.
With AWS CDK, the actual code a developer writes is not the same as the code running during the deployment process.
AWS CDK and CloudFormation are AWS-centric and limited in flexibility for provider-agnostic infrastructure management.
AWS CDK supports only AWS as a cloud provider (AWS-only, no multi-cloud support).
Pulumi supports AWS, Azure, GCP, and on-premises infrastructure for multi-cloud deployment.
AWS CDK debugging is hard due to its reliance on CloudFormation.
Pulumi provides real-time debugging.
AWS CDK supports only TypeScript and Python as languages.
Pulumi supports any programming language.
AWS CDK has slower deployment speed due to CloudFormation.
Pulumi has faster deployment speed due to direct execution.
AWS CDK is hard to trace errors with, offering poor visibility.
Pulumi provides clear deployment state visibility.
AWS CDK's extensibility is limited to the AWS ecosystem.
Pulumi supports custom providers and workflows for extensibility.
AWS CDK uses a CloudFormation state file for state management.
Pulumi uses Pulumi-managed state for state management.
AWS CDK secrets management is limited to AWS Secrets Manager only.
Pulumi supports cross-cloud secret management.
Pulumi treats infrastructure code as a first-class program executed directly during deployment, instead of generating an intermediary format.
With Pulumi, the infrastructure code is the same code that runs during deployment.
Pulumi's provider-agnostic approach allows SST's team to work with a wide range of cloud and on-premises platforms.

SST's Founding Engineer is quoted as saying: "With Pulumi, the deployment process feels like a natural extension of writing code - it's intuitive and powerful and capable of advanced things that traditional IaC tools can't handle."
Pulumi provides improved visibility and debugging capabilities as described at https://www.pulumi.com/product/pulumi-insights/.
Pulumi provides built-in extensibility features such as custom providers and dynamic components.
With SST built on Pulumi, users can manage all of their infrastructure through a single, consistent interface.
Pulumi offers more advanced deployment workflows as described at https://www.pulumi.com/docs/pulumi-cloud/deployments/.
Pulumi provides better visibility into the deployment process as described at https://www.pulumi.com/product/pulumi-insights/.
Pulumi Crosswalk for AWS simplifies 'day one' tasks, as described in the AWS guide at /docs/iac/guides/clouds/aws/.
There is an on-demand workshop titled 'Getting Stated with Infrastructure as Code on AWS' at https://www.pulumi.com/resources/getting-started-with-iac-pulumi-aws/.
Pulumi offers upcoming Platform Engineering or DevOps workshops listed at https://www.pulumi.com/resources/#upcoming.
SST is a framework that makes building modern full-stack applications on your infrastructure easy.
Ion is the code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications.
SST's Ion constructs (or components) are deployed using Pulumi instead of CDK and CloudFormation (CFN).
Once Ion is stable, it will be released as SST v3.
SST leverages Pulumi behind the scenes for its providers and deployment engine.
SST bridges Terraform providers through Pulumi.
SST (Serverless Stack) makes money primarily through its managed service called SST Console.
The SST Console is optional and includes a free tier.
SST primarily relies on SaaS revenue through its managed platform and potentially supplemental income streams like enterprise services and consulting.
SST v3 replaced AWS CDK with an embedded Pulumi engine that talks to Terraform-bridged providers.
SST's embedded Pulumi engine requires no Pulumi account.
When SST rebuilt its deployment engine for v3, it did not write a new engine from scratch.
`sst deploy` runs on an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the actual cloud API calls.
SST's deployment process requires no CDK, no CloudFormation, and no Pulumi account or Pulumi Cloud dependency.
Nitric runs application deployments through the Pulumi engine rather than building its own diff, state, and provider layer from scratch.
Defang runs application deployments through the Pulumi engine rather than building its own diff, state, and provider layer from scratch.
SST is still shipping as of this writing.
The SST team's public attention has broadened to include an AI coding agent called opencode.
SST v3 is the framework's Ion-based rewrite.
SST v3 replaced AWS CDK and CloudFormation with an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the underlying cloud API calls.
Running `sst deploy` needs no separate Pulumi install and no Pulumi account.
The Pulumi engine ships inside the SST CLI.
SST keeps its deployment state in an S3 bucket in the user's own AWS account.
The SST team has repeatedly stated, since the Ion rewrite shipped, that SST's architecture is built on the Pulumi engine.
SST is an open source TypeScript framework from the team formerly known as Serverless Stack.
SST is for building and deploying full-stack applications to AWS and more than 150 other providers.
SST lets users define an app's infrastructure and code together in a single `sst.config.ts` file.
SST provides its own components including functions, queues, buckets, and static sites.
`sst deploy` handles provisioning end to end.
Through 2023, SST's provisioning layer was built directly on AWS CDK and CloudFormation.
In late 2023, the SST team began a rewrite code-named Ion that replaced SST's entire deployment layer.
Ion shipped as SST v3 in mid-2024.
SST v3 (Ion) has been the only supported SST architecture since it shipped in mid-2024.

SST's blog post "Moving away from CDK" states: "Ion is a code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications. The constructs (or components) are defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation (CFN)."

SST's blog post "Moving away from CDK" states: "When you run `sst deploy`, those resources make a call to an embedded Pulumi engine that makes a call to their bridged Terraform provider, and this makes the AWS SDK calls to create your resources."
SST's docs page "What is SST" states: "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine. And Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi."

Gautier Blandin's article "Terraform, Pulumi, SST: a tradeoff analysis" states: "SST uses the Pulumi engine under the hood to manage and provision resources, and lets users write Pulumi code in addition to using SST's constructs, enabling resources with no associated SST constructs to still be defined and deployed."
Kiryl Anoshka's article "SST ditches AWS CDK. Time to move on to Ion" states: "You may notice right away the imports from Pulumi. It means the whole deployment process will be built on Pulumi now."
The published `package.json` for SST's platform package depends on `@pulumi/pulumi`.
The published `package.json` for SST's platform package depends on first-party Pulumi providers for AWS, Cloudflare, and Docker builds, among others.
The published `package.json` for SST's platform package depends on a Pulumiverse Vercel provider.
`sst deploy` reads the user's `sst.config.ts` and resolves SST's own components, and this step is SST's responsibility.
SST's components compile into Pulumi resource declarations, and this step is SST's responsibility.
The Pulumi engine diffs desired vs. actual state, builds a dependency graph, and orders operations.
Terraform-bridged providers translate each resource into cloud API calls, and this is handled by Pulumi's Terraform bridge.
State is written to an S3 bucket in the user's AWS account, and this is SST's responsibility (self-hosted, not Pulumi Cloud).
SST owns the developer-facing layer: the CLI, the component model, and the local dev loop.
Pulumi's engine owns the provisioning mechanics underneath SST: dependency resolution, preview and diff, state tracking, and connectivity to hundreds of provider APIs.
AWS alone exposes hundreds of resource types, each with its own create, update, and delete semantics.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge is Apache-2.0 licensed.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge is built specifically to let projects like SST reuse Terraform's provider ecosystem, adapted for the Pulumi engine, instead of writing and maintaining their own providers.
Pulumi's engine does not require a Pulumi account, a network call to Pulumi Cloud, or any Pulumi-hosted service to run.
Pulumi's Automation API works the same embedded way, for teams embedding Pulumi programs inside their own tools.
The same provider bridge that lets SST use Terraform-bridged providers also lets any Pulumi user consume Terraform providers directly.
Nitric is a cloud-agnostic application framework.
Nitric's own docs state that "all of the direct deployment providers use Pulumi under the hood for their deployments."
Nitric's official providers are built directly on Pulumi's AWS, GCP, and Azure providers.
Defang deploys Docker Compose applications to the cloud.
Defang describes its Pulumi provider as taking "a Compose file, translates it to a Pulumi program, and runs `pulumi up`" to provision the result.
SST users are not Pulumi Cloud customers.
SST's state lives in the user's own S3 bucket, not in Pulumi's hosted service.
SST does not require a Pulumi account to work.
Most SST users never write a line of Pulumi code and work entirely in SST's component model.
SST's constructs compile to Pulumi resources.
Resources that don't have a dedicated SST construct yet can still be defined directly in Pulumi and deployed as part of the same SST app.
The latest SST release, v4.17.1, went out in July 2026.
The `sst` package on npm is pulling roughly 796,000 downloads a week as of this writing.
SST's own team page credits the same team behind opencode.
opencode is an open source AI coding agent.
opencode has grown quickly since launch and now carries a larger following on GitHub than SST itself.
SST's expansion into opencode is a legitimate expansion of what the team works on, not a sign that SST is being abandoned.
SST's dependency on the Pulumi engine hasn't changed as a result of the team's broadened public attention.
If you already run SST, you are already running Pulumi's engine, whether or not you've written a line of Pulumi code yourself.
Pulumi Cloud provides cross-team visibility into infrastructure state.
Pulumi's policy as code provides guardrails that a platform team can enforce centrally.
Pulumi's components feature allows sharing infrastructure patterns across a whole organization rather than just within one SST app.

Since SST v3 (the Ion rewrite, shipped mid-2024), `sst deploy` runs through an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the underlying cloud API calls, replacing SST's earlier architecture on AWS CDK and CloudFormation.
Pulumi's engine is embedded directly in the SST CLI.
SST keeps its own state in an S3 bucket in the user's AWS account rather than in Pulumi Cloud.
Users do not need to install Pulumi separately or create a Pulumi account to deploy an SST app.
SST's components are defined using Terraform providers, but those providers are bridged through the Pulumi engine rather than run through Terraform itself.
SST does not invoke the Terraform CLI or write Terraform state.

Because SST's components compile into Pulumi resource declarations, users can define resources directly with Pulumi for anything that doesn't yet have a dedicated SST construct, and deploy them as part of the same app.
SST shipped v4.17.1 in July 2026.
The `sst` package continues to see roughly 796,000 weekly downloads on npm.
The SST team's broadened public attention to opencode hasn't changed SST's release cadence or its dependency on the Pulumi engine.

Reaching for Pulumi directly makes more sense once a user needs capabilities SST doesn't expose on its own, such as cross-team visibility, policy enforcement, or infrastructure shared across more than one application, since that's the same engine SST already runs on.
The `anomalyco/sst` GitHub repository was formerly named `sst/sst`.

The `platform/package.json` in the `anomalyco/sst` repository, verified September 2026, lists `@pulumi/pulumi`, `@pulumi/aws`, `@pulumi/cloudflare`, `@pulumi/command`, `@pulumi/docker-build`, `@pulumi/random`, `@pulumi/tls`, and `@pulumiverse/vercel` as direct dependencies.
npm download stats for `sst` show 796,291 downloads for the week of September 5-11, 2026.
The `anomalyco/opencode` GitHub repository's star count was observed in September 2026.
This post is related to the post "aws-cdk-vs-pulumi-why-sst-switched".
"AWS CDK vs Pulumi: Why SST Chose Pulumi" tells the fuller story of SST's move off CDK, from SST's side.
"How Pulumi IaC Works" covers the engine mechanics referenced throughout this post.
"Introducing: Support For Using Any Terraform Provider with Pulumi" describes the bridge that SST and others build on.
The Automation API page describes how other tools embed Pulumi the same way SST does.
